speaker: Sam Schrager
words: This conversation with Glenn Gilder took place at his home near Troy on May 22nd, 1975. The interviewer is Sam Schrager.

speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
words: My showmanship. He is a buffalo hunter, I think. They claim he hunted for the railroads, but then everybody hunted for the railroads. I have an idea that if Bill Cotey went out to get a buffalo for the railroad, it probably took some Indian kid along to do the shooting and the skinning and he got the glory. I didn't like him. There was no sincerity to him.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: It's a funny thing that he's the one that people think about when they think about what the West was really like, you know?

speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
words: Well, there hasn't been anybody who had more ballyhoo and he promoted his show from Texas to Dakota to Madison Square Garden to Europe and he was a showman, a promoter. He was in it for the glory of the almighty dollar. Well, that's my opinion. You know, somebody else got a different opinion. Maybe one of the others could be right.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I'll bet you're right. I'll bet you are. It's just funny. It seems to me like the story of what the West is really like is something that most people don't even know about. That's what they think.

speaker: Glen or Agnes Gilder
words: Devoto. I don't have that one. I've written up the West of any man that I know of. There are others that have got this man from Texas. I'm trying to think of his name.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Dobie?

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: Yes… he's good. Oh, he is awful good. I've read every book I could get that he has written. I've enjoyed every minute of it. Frank Dobie.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you think the truth about the West is better than the fiction about it?

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: Yes. Yes… the truth about the West doesn't end up on the basis of a lot of good novels. The funny thing is that it was made up and segregated into agriculture, mining, milling, fishing, logging, lumbering. And all good subjects, if they're handled good, they make a good book. I like all those up there… some railroading, logging.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: It seems to me that 95 % of the stuff about the West that you read is all about the cowboys and the cattle on the range. I can't quite figure that one out.

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: Well, it was here. It was here. The eastern version of the West, he came through the prairies dates and seen that. There have been some remarkably good stories written on wheat farming and homesteading. Fisher from South Idaho, have you ever got a hold of anything?

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: A little bit. I read that mountain man of his that you had.

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: Well, I didn't think that was one of them. He wrote of the railroad coming in and he wrote a novel or two on homesteading. He took it from the day they went out there to the homestead. There was another one, a fellow by the name of Estes wrote a book about the country just south and east of Denver. One of the best examples I think I've read of it.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What is it that makes that kind of a book work? What makes it be a real successful book?

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: You know, these books haven't really hit the top bracket because they are so darn close to the truth. They leave out the fiction, the thrilling part. They are thinking of it seriously. I don't know, I couldn't answer. Yeah, I don't know.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Have you read any of those, you read one of those Davis books, H .L. Davis, I gave you that, Honey in the Horn, I think. Yeah. Did you like that one?

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: Pretty good. It was fiction. Yeah. Yeah. He took, the basis of his story was taken from what looks like west of the wide Missouri. Oh, books, books, books, books. The millions of them in the library are just throwing away the good ones and keeping the junk. Throwing the good ones in the dump. You know, after a book begins to, isn't in demand anymore, away she goes. They put a new cover on it. It might be hit the market as a best seller.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I'll tell you, you know.

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: You haven't got this turned on do you?

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, how do you think I get all the good stuff that people tell me? That's the only way. I'll tell you though, Glen, there have been more, more good stories that I've heard from talking to people around here that I've never seen in books. Never hardly, well, hardly anything like them in books.

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: You know. It's not, it's not.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: When you told me there was a hell of a story out there, and all I had to do was ask people about it, you were really right. Because that's all I did.

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: Well. Those are. There's an interesting history in this country and it's, it's hard to get all of it from any one point. You've got to see so awful many. I might not give you a start. George Nichols got a story over there that, there's a book. In the Butterfield, the same way.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I don't think any two stories are close to the same. Any two stories that I've heard, you know, everybody's life is different. More than you'd expect being from the same area.

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: They live on adjoining farms and the interests be a little bit different. Well, that's the way it goes. Oh, did you have quite a talk with, uh, Irie?

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Mm-hmm. Spent an hour or so with him. Well. It was a good talk. I'm gonna go back and talk to him again.

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: I would, and when you do, if you could get him with, uh, Frank Herzog. Get the Prune Joe story. Get the Pippen Gilbert story on cleaning up that meadow up there in Kenlan Homestead.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: And what's that story?

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: That's a good one. Well, it's so long ago since I've heard it. I don't know whether I can or not to get it exactly right, but, uh, when the Potlatch first come into the country, they put a camp there close to Bennett Mill, south and up on the hill. And they put another one up there on the, uh, on a part of the land that Jess Euler owns that he got from Ben Stewart. Stewart got it from Bill Helmer. And that was camp three. And then camp four was less than a mile from there. I don't know why. Different time. And, uh, Gil, evidently, was a foreman for the, kind of overall them. But they, they wanted to land their logs off of Jerome Creek on the bank of the Blue Silver. Well, that put it on Kenlan's place. I don't know whether Gil didn't know who owned the land or what. But he went in there and started cutting the logs and they started landing them along the river there, cutting the brush and cleaning it all up. And they filled that meadow, as you can tell, with ten acres there, solid with logs. And they got ready to put the drive on. And Kenlan said, no, you can't move these logs until you pay for the privilege of putting them on that land. And by golly, they didn't. They cleaned his land and then they paid him for it, which is all exactly what I'd have done to, I think, under the circumstances.

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: Those things.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, who's this Prune Joe? Prune Joe?

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: Yeah. He's Bill Helmer's ranch foreman. Uh, you'd get that story from Frank. Frank's a little older and knew him a little better than I did.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, tell me what you heard, anyway. Well, I didn't hear it. I knew the guy.

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: Why they called him Prune Joe, I don't know. I've heard a dozen different stories. He made wine out of prunes. He was an Austrian. Or was it half of the diet? Prunes and beans? I couldn't say, but that was his name. He went in there and cleared up all the land. For Bill Helmer, he cleaned up... 120... Cleared up better than 200 acres out of heavy timber and put it in crop. But, of course, he had access to all the damn money he wanted. I don't know whether Bill Helmer had that much money or not, but there was always a crew there. A lot of men. I don't know. I... You'd get that story from Frank.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, Helmer was their main cruiser, right? Helmer was their main cruiser?

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: Yeah, yeah. Head cruiser, yeah.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you know what the story is on how the mill came to Potlatch?

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: Well, that's where Deary wanted it. You see, the mill was the first to come to Moscow… and they were putting a railroad from Moscow... They were going to get up into the Bovill area some way. And they'd done a lot of work on it. They made that cut where they had that second... Well, that sanitary landfill between Troy and Moscow. That was the cut for the company's railroad. And when they got that far,… they were having a meeting in Moscow. It was raining and Bill Helmer came in there and Deary... I guess they were sopping wet they'd been out on the brush all day. And Deary was kind of angry. He told them to stop it. He took a map, he poked it down through that... He poked a pencil down through that map and he says, That mill was going to be right there and he poked it down where Potlatch is. We had a grade clear over there.

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: This going from Moscow to Bovill wouldn't have got any excessive amount of timber. But going from Palouse to Bovill, they went through the whole thing. It was not a grade practically. So that's where the railroad went and that's where the mill went.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Didn't you tell me he had a story? I mean, didn't he have a reason about it? About Moscow? Didn't you tell me in Moscow there wasn't enough water in Moscow?

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: There wasn't a pond, there wasn't anything there to influence it. No, Deary was right. You know, this is all written up. By who or what end? I don't know, I don't remember. The Miller boat couldn't. Possibly, part of it. The fellow that told me this story was the engineer. His name was Talbot. He's dead now. He told me that story about 10 or 15 years ago. He was there.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Before they started the town there at Potlatch, you were telling me that Palouse was really the big center. It was really an important place for the people in the country. Well, it was. It was the only.

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: There was a stage stop in the post office at Woodfell, a stage stop in the post office at Hampton, and one at Kennedy Ford. There used to be little. I guess they handled the mail and probably, part of the time, a few groceries. But if you wanted any groceries and lived at Harvard or Avon or whatever, you had to go to Flus after it. Dover team. Sometimes that took quite a while. Some of them had teams that go down there pretty darn quick. Go from Harvard to Potlatch and back and do their shopping in two hours and a half. Can't do that with a Model T Ford… well, that's right.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What was that road like when you were growing up there?

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: About six inches wider than a wagon. Mud axle deep all winter and dust halfway up all summer. There were a few days when it was pretty nice, like early in the spring, late in the fall. Some of those horses made some awful runs. Accidents. Things like that.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You mean running into each other on that road?

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: No, no. Say that somebody got hurt and they sent somebody after a doctor. It didn't take them long to go twenty-five miles. They just kicked that horse in high gear and he had to butt them and stamina to stay and make the trip. When he got that one made, he took a feed oats and a drink of water and went back.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What made your parents decide to come out here to this area? Where did you come from?

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: My mother came from Iowa. She was just a little girl when she came, I guess. A young girl. My dad must have been about nineteen, eighteen or nineteen years old. He came from Sault Ste. Marie to Dakota. He didn't like it. He'd heard about the Palouse Country, so he came on the Palouse. He had itchy feet, I guess. That's about the only reason I know of. The West had been told and played up by the railroads and people that had gone back. It was so fantastically wonderful. Every Easterner would have came out here if he could have.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I wonder why he didn't like Dakota.

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: Oh, oh, droughts and grasshoppers kicked him out of there. There was nothing left after two things got through with him. Oh, I don't know. The three boys, four of them, came west. One came to Sweetgrass in Montana and stayed there. They had a very successful life. Charlie came to Palouse and Albin because Dad had came, partly. And then one went on over to Vancouver.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: About when did your father get out here, you know?

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: Must have been about 90 or 91. My mother, her folks, must have come out about 85 or somewhere around in that area.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Who is that?

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: She was born in 87, maybe about 85 or 86. Well, some person in there. I don't know.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Seems like this country was one of the last pieces that was real good land to get settled up. I mean, in the Palouse, the whole Palouse country. Sure a lot better than Dakota.

speaker: Agnes Gilder
words: What's Lorraine's husband's middle name?

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: Well, I think that's right.

speaker: Agnes Gilder
words: Lorraine, huh?

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: Yes. It was kind of slow getting in here, but when they did get there, they stayed. There's a book up there, Whitman County History, that's awful good. It tells the dates and all these things. Settling Pullman and Union Flat.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Your folks didn't move up by Harvard at first, right? They were someplace?

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: No, they had homesteaded down at Hooper.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Where?

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: Hooper. About, oh, maybe 10 miles on the side of the cross. And he stayed there five or six years and broke up that prairie. Well, he knew he didn't have very good wheat land and he wanted to raise wheat. So he put in two or three crops that weren't very good and finally he got a good crop. And that crop sold a place, so he got out of there and came up to Palouse. And then up to Harvard.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did he buy the place there or did he, he bought it… uh huh.

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: He bought 80 acres from Potlatch Lumber Company and 120 from Bill Helmer. Well, it was logged over, it was mostly brush, he cleared it up. The hard way with team of horses and... Oh, team of horses and a grubble.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you get to do much of that yourself?

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: You betcha. A boy was a man about that time when he was about 10 or 11, 12 years old. He could drive a team where he was as good as a man. That's the way it worked. You can take them along to know how to run one end of a crosscut saw. But the next thing he got to be expert with was an axe. He could just about plane a board with an axe.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Can I have a cigarette, Glenn?

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: Oh, you sure can. You betcha. But we just made kind of a general plan and traded out if we could, when we could. Sometimes they'd get a piece of grum cleared up way up in June. They'd get through with it, you know, maybe a half an acre or an acre. It's too late to put it in grain. They'd plow it and put it in spuds or somewhere to follow it. Put it in crop next year. On a tiny scale it was just like they worked it after they got on a bigger scale. Only it was a tiny scale, I'm telling you. Half an acre was important. Now, what do you think of it? It'd be in a fence corner.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Seems like now the farmer's got to put every square inch under if he can.

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: Yeah, they're doing it. But we... My dad had the idea that another acre of wheat was a way of getting there. I've never agreed with him. I never have seen the day when I considered wheat a good crop. I don't know why. I'd sooner have hay or a cow or some other way. But I just... In my life I just trusted wheat. I thought it was unreliable. It was unsecure. Unless you could just be in the very biggest bracket. And it's probably partly the reason some of the very biggest ones. During the 1920s and long in there were the first ones to go broke. At least they had wonderful auction sales. Thirty, fifty head horses. All their harness and gear and rigging and equipment. A good time was had by all.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: The wheat market went down fast after the first war, right?

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: After all wars. I think the country got hurt the worst after World War I. Unless it's being hurt the worst right now… i don't know.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: But your father believed in wheat. Probably most people did.

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: No, not most. They all... That was a cash crop. Grain. Grain. Grain. And they'd come here and bust it the next. Make it again the next year and bust the next. Up and down.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did your father work out when you were a kid?

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: Yeah… everybody did… he worked at any job he could find around close to home. Maybe a day or two or maybe a month. There wasn't any work in the wintertime. Seriously ever. But during that time he'd build or make friends. Do something. He never was idle, that's for damn sure. He'd be more ambitious than I've ever been. He'd be ready to start at six o 'clock in the morning. He wasn't ready to quit until six o 'clock at night either. I've never been... I don't know. I've never been... That much to crowd things.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: How many brothers and sisters? How big was the family?

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: Eight… wouldn't it… one, two... No, wait a minute. Six. There were three girls and three boys.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, two parents.

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: I was thinking of my own family. There was a hard deal to support that many. A kid nowadays in school has more laid out on him in one year than that whole family had in two. But we didn't miss anything. We didn't... Somehow or other you can't miss anything that you don't know exists. What is it? How are you going to say it?

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Ignorance is bliss.

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: We should have blessed her then. Well, we had food and clothes. There was a shortage of that. But the clothes weren't fancy. They were just common everyday old work clothes. But they were warm and most of the time dry. Ten dollars would buy all the clothes I needed for winter when I was about twelve, thirteen years old. I know because I earned that much and bought my own clothes. I had all I needed. Of course there was a difference between a tuxedo and a pair of overalls.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What did you do to earn that money?

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: I generally drove horses for somebody putting in a crop. Or anything. Not the way those kids did earn money though. They'd drive horses for somebody. They'd sit on the seat you know. I had nothing to see a twelve, thirteen year old kid driving six or eight horses. I could handle them just as good as a great grandpa. But anyway, they didn't have to have six or eight if they could. Two or any unit of it. It depends on the size of the operation and where it was. They didn't have six horse teams around Harvard but they did around below potlatch.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Would you have in a way a stock when you were ten or a youngster?

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: About three horses and twelve cows I imagine. Maybe two or three brutes out and a few chickens. That's about it. Then they got more as the place grew larger as the cleared land increased. Each of those things increased as there was feed for them. But it started small and had to start small. You couldn't buy hay, you couldn't buy grain. In the first place you didn't have the money and in the second place it wasn't for sale.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Would you say it was pretty much self sufficient? The farm?

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: Just as near as possible. Yes. And it was pretty much possible. We take our own wheat to a mill someplace. At first they didn't grind it only just into a good grade of hog feed but they chopped and made food. I think they took a sack of wheat to Palouse to Old Man Hunsberger there in the grist mill. I think he sent them back a sack of flour, fifty pounds, for each sack of wheat. He also sent back a farina and bran. That was their flour. Just practically growing on the place. Spuds, milk, butter, eggs, vegetables. There wasn't much to buy. Coffee, sugar, tomato and salt most of the time. Bacon powder with awful expense. About fifty cents a can for a two or three pound can. It was a good life time. I don't think any of us got any kick or any rugrats on it. We did our work and we had our time to play just the same as we've got now I think even more.

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: We made our own amusement, dances, parties, swimming, sleigh rides. My brother and I used to like to walk and climb a hill the highest hill we could see. It didn't matter if it was ten miles away we'd climb it. We'd go fishing, hunting, trapping, those. We found a lot of things. Then there were just everyday occurrences that people pay two hundred and fifty dollars a week to do now. You know what they do? Come out from the city and pay two hundred and three hundred and fifty dollars a week to do what we played at as kids. And all of our life. Frank Herzog, he was a better trapper than I am. He got back and got the bobcats and bear. His dad got fifteen one summer. Fifteen. Bear, big ones. They used to be thick. His dad used to come by our place on his way to and from his traps and he'd always leave a quarter of a bear steak for us. About once a week.

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: He caught a bobcat one time and he had it in his head and he was going to take it home to skin it. The damn thing come to in the sack and scratched him a little bit. He just went on home with it and put a collar around his neck and tied it in the back of the woodshed and that cat was around there for a long time. But the kids used to, we used to trap muskrats and mink. A few coyotes, quite a few weasels when they get white. And they made fifteen, twenty dollars in a winter's time.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: How'd you get around mostly in the winter when you were a kid Glen?

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: ... Of course we had our saddle horses too but any horses we had were certainly broke to ride and they furnished our transportation. But mostly we walked or hell we seldom walk we run. If I was going to go to Troy when I was fifteen or eighteen years old I wouldn't walk. I'd run two thirds away in there. Think nothing of it.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: How would you go?

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: Straight through. Didn't follow the roads. Go straight through. When we had these coyote traps back up there, there was three of us in on it and we'd run. Seventy eight miles around the string. And each of us had stepped in the guy ahead of him's tracks without disturbing that track. That was a game. You'd get pretty darned expert at it.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: In winter did you snowshoe much?

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: Some… if needed be. We generally had snowshoes or skis but we made them ourselves if we did have.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: This route you'd take to Troy from Harvard that interests me. How you'd go over the divide there and get into town here. I know it's not very far by the land but it sure is far nowadays.

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: When I moved over here to this place I moved from Harvard here. The road came just as it does now but after you got up there, or while I prayed we used to live, the road cut through by white pine mill and we'd come up right in front of Hans' house. And then we'd have to go down the highway and down to ... and then get off the highway and come in here. But I moved the whole outfit with accepting I think a load of stock and a load or two hay. Anyway I moved it all of course, household goods and foolishly moved my old junk machinery over here which I shouldn't have done. I should have sold it over there and bought it back over here because that would have been possible. Didn't need much.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What year was this when you moved here? Here?

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: 39. 39… there was no snow there, no sleighing. It was all wagon. One morning I thought I had sleighing enough to get a load over here and I loaded the sled and pulled out over there. And I got to Avon, up this side of Avon and the snow just simply gave out. It melted. And I struggled all day to get up there just about where Garrelle Price lives and unhooked, left my sled setting and went back and stayed all night with Dwight Corey and got a team from him the next morning and come on and move that rig on over here. And I took the wagon for the balance of it. There wasn't any snow, the ground didn't get white all winter. Two or three days. And the next winter it made up for it.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What about the fishing up there when you were a kid?

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: It was good… it was real good. Any place. You never got big fish. Oh, 16, 18 inches long but there was... You got enough in a little while to have a good meal on them. We used to go up to Strychnine and get in the creek and wade down to Third Park and get out and take and wrap the fish in a couple of, three or four thimbleberry leaves. And just make a mud bowl around him. Put him in the coals. Put a spud in there with him, alongside of him in the ashes. Covered up good. Egg or two. It was a pretty good meal. In the afternoon we'd probably fish on down to a couple of miles. But we'd have nice messes. The meat was mostly about 8-10 inches long. I think the meat was just yellow salmon.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Had that country up in there been logged when you were a kid?

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: No, they were logging it. Of course they got done around Harvard. They got pretty well done by about 1910 or 1912. The pot lights had pulled out of there and gone up. Old Helmer up in that area. Bovill. But they had, there was always some logging going on. After we kids got a little size on us, what we used to saw during the summer for some of those little loggers around close.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: We used to run into those old miners back in that country.

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: Like hoodoos… sure. Sure, we loved them. Those kids did. Steffens, Billy, Connors, Pete Dufner, Airsmith, Jack Connors. We used to go up there and work for them. Lou Watson did the assessment work for some of them. For Lou Watson we did several years. But they were old bachelors and they liked kids. And on Friday night after school we'd quite often go up there and stay Friday night, Saturday night. And then Sunday we walked back home. We had some good friends up there among them old fellows. They liked to see us kids coming. And us kids liked to go.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did they mind having you around their diggings and stuff like that?

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: Oh no, we didn't bother them. We soon learned that there were limitations of what privileges we had while we were visiting one of them. But we'd just play around the woods or cut woods for them. It looked like if anything needed to be done we'd do it, you know. They'd visit with us. I think they enjoyed it. I know they did.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Those guys must have been pretty lonely by themselves sometimes being alone and all that.

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: It didn't bother them. That's the way they wanted it. No, they'd live there within a quarter of a mile or half a mile of each other and wouldn't go in each other's cabin once a year. Most of them. We used to get paid pretty good to take a team and wagon and take their groceries up to them once or twice a year. We used to do that with Doffner. Once or twice with Steffens and for Lou Watson. We used to have a regular run there. We'd have to go up there about every two or three weeks all summer. Go up one day and back the next.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Just your family? Your family?

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: No, no. Just one or two of us boys.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Where were they located? The miners that you're speaking of? Have you been up? I know the area pretty well.

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: Do you know where the North Fork and the South Fork of the Palouse Fork up there? Well, there was one below that fork about a half a mile or a little bit near by Livingston. And then the rest of them were at the North Fork. And this one back in there where Whedon saw the thing and they were about a mile. And then Steffens and Doffner and O 'Connor just scattered along.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did they do very good up there mining? Hmm? Did they do very good up there mining?

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: Doug Heirsmith told me one time that they took out six dollars a day while they could wash on their claim. Thought it would be two of them working. That was pretty good money then. The rest of them were mum. You didn't know what they did. I'll never tell you. They didn't leave any tremendous estates, so I know that.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you think, Glenn, that they were different from the real kind of difference in the kind of people they were from the settlers? The kind of people that settled and had farms? Were they a special breed?

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: No, I don't think so. They just wanted to be independents of the rest of the world. And they sure as hell were. No, they weren't. They just didn't marry. That's about the only difference I can see in them. Oh, there was two of them. John English and Jack Connor. Jean Wiedenthal. Three of them got married. And then, Livingston was married when he came in there… ted,… i can't think of his name. He lived south of town about three or four miles… strome?

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You've got to tell me what you mean by independent. They didn't want to be messed with more than most people?

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: Well, I think they had that, but they didn't want to be dependent on anybody or anything. And I don't think they wanted anybody to be dependent on them from the way it worked out. They were nice old guys… cranky sometimes… most of the time, though. I'll tell you, they were cranky with each other. But, I never seen a day when they weren't friendly with my brothers or I or our families. When they happened to be up in that area huckleberrying or fishing or something like that. Sometimes they'd go out with us and show us where there's a good patch or... I'm glad to see us, I think. I acted like they were.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Oh, those men stayed up in there for many years, didn't they? Do you think they've had among themselves many stories about hidden gold, lost mines?

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: No, I don't. No. Well, there was a doctor in Palouse had a lost mine, a lost wheelbarrow mine up there on the west side of Gold Hill. He blew that up pretty big, but actually it was just an abandoned mine and there was no great lot of ore there. The Caricos and Gillums and others were in there. There was lots of prospecting done. For deep mines, after the gold rush was over, you see, there was quite a little gold rush in that area at first. And then after the country was worked out, there were some deep prospects went in. One on Baby Grand and the Metis Paul and the Gold Bug. And the Caricos, or whoever that lost wheelbarrow was, I don't remember. But they were deep. But they never hit enough to justify their keeping going.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You knew Penelle, didn't you… yes.

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: Real well. He was in the Gold Bug.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What's the deal on him? They say he had quite a bit of worthless mining stock that a lot of people bought. Nobody wants to admit they did buy it themselves, but they say everybody else did.

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: Well, the Gold Bug showed pretty good prospecting to miners. I wouldn't know. Nothing about it. But Ed... There were quite a number involved in it. They actually believed in it. And they worked it for years. And when they get short of money, they go out and sell stock. And they work that up and heat it up and go sell some more. But it never turned out well. But the Northups in the Gold Bug, they worked the same deal. They didn't have money enough to develop it. They had a faith that it was going to eventually turn good. And they worked for years and get every dollar they could. Selling stock or trading, dickering. To keep going. Keep going down, down. But it just... both of these places shipped ore. And that's bought quite a bit. But they couldn't make it pay. It wasn't rich enough. Too expensive to mine it, perhaps.

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: Those men... works up in the Bunker Hill… marvin Darryl… and he still has a stock in the Mizpah and some several claims in there on Poor Man Creek. He spent his life in mining in the big mines up there. And he still got his confidence and faith in it… so, who knows… someday they might… marvin Darryl is a man that... I think he knows what he's talking about. He's not trying to sell me any. The fact is, I don't think he would sell me any. But he gets all of it he can get his hands on. And there's others up there right in with him.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: The Mizpah took quite a bit of copper out of there, didn't they?

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: Yeah, a fella hauled it out with a six horse team wagon. Trail wagon. I don't think. I don't know. Maybe they trucked some of it out. But I think it was all done before they were trucks.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Oh, Glen, what's the story that you know about that Duff Wagner feud on the creek there?

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: Well, I don't think anybody knows too much about that. But old Billy Duff was sleeping sound as could be. And old Wagner Charlie came in and opened the door and jumped on top of him. If I had one shot down the long side of his head, he'd have done a star beating him with that pistol. Now, I don't know what caused that. I knew both of them and I've talked to both of them about it. I don't think they had had any argument before that. I don't think they'd had any particular trouble. They never I can't see any justifiable reason for it happening, but that's just what happened. And after he beat him a little bit, he got up off him, went back outside and went home and I don't think there was two words said all the time he was in there. And Duff's what it went for him. I had him arrested and they had a trial over it.

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: Duff packed a pistol on his hip though from that day till the day he died. He put that on the first thing he got up in the morning and he slept with it under his pillow. But they never had any more trouble. That was it. I don't know.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Neither of them ever told you their side of it?

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: A Wagner wouldn't say very much. He didn't say, well nothing of any consequence. He didn't want to talk about it. Duff didn't mind. But that's just about all the story that Duff told. He was back to visit. He used to come and get me and my team or my dad's team, whichever were available. Every spring. And we'd repair all the roads between… well, between where the highway is now, there are Kinmans and Cohens. Into the head of the roads, both on the heads of the Palouse River. And we'd grade that road with a little old horse grader that you could put in there and pick up and carry. Four horses on it. I drove them. And we'd fix a culvert here and maybe a ditch there. Maybe take out a stump someplace. But, well, it generally took about 10-12 days to repair that road all up real good. I don't remember what I got for wages. $3 or $4 a day I think for me and the team.

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: Pretty good steak.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did the county pay for that?

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: Mm-hmm… i had to walk down to Princeton to get my check for that. Old name of Hawkins was a treasurer of the road district for a few years. And then I think he died and I thought of my name while Lenhart took it over then. But I know many times I've walked down from home to Princeton to get that check.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Just where was the home place from Harvard?

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: You know when you're driving out going to Micah, you go up from the time you leave the store there at Harvard, you go up quite a long grade. Just a slight little grade. When you get to the top of that, you look straight east a mile and that's it. There's a White House and Big Barn, just oilers down to the hill and then my folks place was back on top of the hill… august Karl Mance… his mother owned that now. There's just two farms in that area now where there used to be one, two, three, four, there used to be five. Two guys who got the whole country in there.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was it a real community when you were a kid growing up there?

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: Yeah, Harvard was a hub. There was one pretty darn nice store, hotel,… blacksmith shop, liver stable and an ice cream parlor. That was it… but it was a community center and about one or two nights a week there'd be something going on, something social. They had a good range,… dances, parties, literaries. They had the church in the school house until, gee I believe it must have been pretty near 1925 or such a matter before they built a church up there. They were a religious community but they never had money to build a church I guess. They were always a school house.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Is the school house where the community get togethers were mostly?

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: There or the Grange Hall, yeah. That's the only two places there were. Grange and dances and parties, literary. There was always something. They had a lot of good times. No friction, they all enjoyed themselves. I don't think there was such a thing as jealousy or friction in the entire neighborhood. For a Grange Master they'd elect just about anybody, this one, always a different one. They were always satisfied with the way it went. The church in Sunday School was about the same way. I never heard any arguments or anything.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Hi, how are you doing… when they had parties… would they be like big feeds too?

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: Oh yeah, sure… fourth of July and Lincoln's birthday and Christmas. And when anything going on like that, there didn't just a fugle. Everybody in the neighborhood went. If there was good skating, and there used to be some tremendous skating, about six o 'clock there would be 150 people skating around there. Come from every direction. Believe me, them people that grew up around the Great Lakes or up in Minnesota, those states, talk about skaters, they don't have many better than the shows they have there in Spokane.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What would one be like? Like everybody would skate until dark and then go in and have a big feed, that kind of thing?

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: Just about anything you can imagine. They might go and play games for a while.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: They have those party games like Skip to My Lou and things like that?

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: They had to think of something and they thought of everything. Crazy games, all kinds, anything. Spin the platter and what the heck, heavy, heavy hangs over your head. I see a bunch of people in there all ages playing games that were invented for kids, I guess. But darn it we had fun. Sleigh rides in the wintertime. I tried to get Carl to tell you about a sleigh ride one night. Did he tell you about having a chicken feed at the end of it?

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You know, I can't remember now what it was that he said. I know.

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: Just involve chicken feed to what they do now and of course they had to solve all these pros and cons for everybody that's running for office. Price of wheat in the war news, just the same as it is now. The only thing is now, you see one or two guys at a time, they used to get in there, ten or fifteen of them. I don't see how they got so much to talk about out of them two little papers, but they did. Now we got the television and radio papers. Don't seem to cover it any better. But I do think that the things that they cover now are more disgusting, discouraging and disturbing than they were then. But they had the trends, it was similar.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What do you think they thought about prohibition? That always seemed like such a dumb one to me.

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: You know, it never affected that area up there very much. The dances were seldom, if ever, anybody took a bottle to them. And there were, I think there were two stills in the area, but the market was outside of the area. But they never got excited, there wasn't a drinking crowd up there, there was a few of them that had to take a drink. Most any of them, they might make some wine or, but they didn't take it very seriously, there were no serious drinkers up there. But you get down to Potlatch and it changed, it was different, they were pretty serious about it down there. But anyway, there was two stills in that country up there, and I don't think there ever was any more. If there had been, I'd known about it. By the gods around Potlatch and the rest of Latah County, there was one in almost every section.

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: Once in a great while, some of us kids would get a hold of a bottle full of white ..., and probably about 15 or 20 of us would smell the cork and be drunker in hell. But that's about all I'm up to.

speaker: Unknown Speaker
words: Just a second, is Sue here?

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: Yeah. Upstairs, just a second. No, that was the community up there… sue? Sue… a hundred percent.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you hear her up there? I think maybe she might have gone out. A rosemary I think went someplace. She's not in the house now and I don't know where she is.

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: Okay. Well, who it is, call her back.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What about young people going together? Many marriages come out of the young people in the community, meeting each other up there.

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: Oh yeah, sure… most of them. Married right around the community there. A few of us didn't. I went clear down to Potlatch. Most of them got their girls closer to home. A lot of rivalry. Some friction. A few fights, but not too many. Oh yeah, there are many, many, many of them. People around there. Amott, Cochran, Canfield. Oh heck, I assume most of them. Ninety percent of them are just married right in the neighborhood.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What was the courting like in those days?

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: Well, I think it was just about the same as it is now. It either walked or drove a team in buggy. Went to dances, shows, picnics, whatever. Church, mostly that. I was important. Church was important. That's where all the big girls went. So all the big boys did too. I don't think that's changed too much. Means of transportation is about all. And the cost. Used to cost four bits to take a girl out for nights in her attainment. Now they say it takes fifty dollars. I don't know.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: They don't shivaree anymore.

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: That's too bad… boy, they sure shivareed us. Damn near tore our house down. It was just an old tie paper shack. I thought they were going to tear it down. I had a bucket of milk. I just got through milking. It was set on a drain board. I hadn't skimmed it yet. About three gallons of it. And a couple of guys got back behind that with a fence post that was banging on the wall. And they tipped that bucket of milk over on the kitchen floor. And Agnes and I had seen them coming. We weren't in the house. We were out with the shivaree crowd and they didn't know it. We were just a shivaree and Glenn and Agnes to beat the band. But when they tipped that bucket of milk over on the floor the whole crowd tripped right in. Waited through it. Put in an evening of having a lot of fun. But the house was a mess.

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: Three gallons of milk goes quite a ways mixed with the mud. They all met up down to the highway I guess. I don't know. But anyway we seen them coming and we went outside and hid. And when they came up in the yard with them we just mixed right in with them. It was dark. They couldn't tell the difference. We were just a shivaree and to beat the band. That was part of it.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Yeah it seems like a good custom to me.

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: And then they had their showers for their kids. Oh I don't know. They had fun. They were hard. They were honest. I think there was... I didn't know anybody on the Palouse River that wasn't admirable.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: That speaks real highly of people.

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: That's the way they were. We Palouse see each other now from Lewiston to Spokane or wherever. They're scattered. About two or three times a year one of them tell me that... Or tell my friends that were with me, don't ever believe that fella. He'd drink a drink out of the Palouse River and anybody that drinks out of the Palouse River will never tell the truth again. But by golly, if a man gave you his word up there, you could take it if it was for a dollar or a thousand or whatever it was. You wouldn't need a note.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I suppose I should be getting going.

speaker: Glen Gilder
words: Well, I suppose you... I hope I've helped.
